Cry
KRī
n. and v. (rendering Hebrew ts'āqâh and sh''âh, Greek krazō and boaō)
From Old French crier, from Latin quiritare, to wail or call for help — said to derive from calling upon the Quirites, the citizens, for aid. The Hebrew ts'āqâh is a shriek or outcry wrung out by distress rather than a considered petition, and the Greek krazō is likewise a raw, loud call. Scripture's point is that this — not eloquence — is what God undertakes to hear.

Biblical Definition

A cry in Scripture is prayer stripped of composure, and it is the form of prayer God is most often said to hear. The Exodus begins with one, and the divine response is described in a sequence of verbs that leaves nothing to chance: “I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows” (Exo 3:7). God sees, hears, and knows — and then comes down. The psalms make the same connection a settled rule of God's dealings: “The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles” (Psa 34:17). Hearing is not always the same as answering at once, and David records a wait without complaining of it: “I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry” (Psa 40:1) — the inclining being the picture of One who bends down to catch what is said. The New Testament traces the cry to its source in the believer and finds the Spirit there, so that the rawest prayer is also the most evidently supernatural: “For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father” (Rom 8:15). The word for slaves crying under taskmasters becomes the word for sons crying to a Father. And Scripture records that the cry of the oppressed rises whether or not anyone means it as prayer: the blood of Abel cried from the ground, and the hire of the defrauded labourer cries in the ears of the Lord of sabaoth.

Webster 1828 Definition

To call loudly, especially in distress; an outcry, clamour, or lamentation; and in Scripture the cry of the oppressed which God hears and answers, and the cry of Abba, Father, which the Spirit of adoption prompts in His children.

expand to see more

CRY, v. 1. To utter a loud voice; to speak, call or exclaim with vehemence.

2. To call importunately; to utter a loud voice with earnestness, by way of prayer or entreaty.

3. To utter a loud voice in weeping; to lament aloud.

4. n. A loud utterance; especially, the utterance of a sudden or violent emotion; an outcry.

5. In Scripture, the cry of the oppressed, which God regards. Exod. 3. The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth. Psalm 34.

Key Scripture

Exodus 3:7 — "And the LORD said, I have surely seen the affliction of my people which are in Egypt, and have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows;"

Psalm 34:17 — "The righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them out of all their troubles."

Psalm 40:1 — "To the chief Musician, A Psalm of David. I waited patiently for the LORD; and he inclined unto me, and heard my cry."

Romans 8:15 — "For ye have not received the spirit of bondage again to fear; but ye have received the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father."

Modern Corruption

Prayer is reduced to composed and articulate performance, so that the raw cry of grief is treated as immature; and the cry of the oppressed is either ignored by the comfortable or annexed to political frameworks Scripture does not use.

expand to see more

Where prayer is judged by fluency, the cry disappears. A congregation trained to admire well-turned petitions learns that grief must be composed before it can be brought, and the psalms — a third of which are laments, some of them ending without resolution — become unusable. Scripture's pattern is the opposite. It preserves prayers that shriek: how long, O LORD? my God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me? out of the depths have I cried unto thee. The Lord Jesus Himself, in the days of his flesh, offered up prayers and supplications with strong crying and tears. A theology that cannot make room for that has made prayer a performance rather than the voice of a child, and has quietly excluded the suffering at the moment they most need to speak.

The cry of the oppressed suffers a double corruption. The comfortable dismiss it, forgetting that Scripture treats such cries as entering God's ears whether or not the crier is pious — the wages of the defrauded reaper cry, and the LORD hears them. But it is equally a corruption to annex those cries to frameworks that replace Scripture's categories with an oppressor-oppressed binary determined by group identity, so that guilt and innocence are read off membership rather than off conduct before God. The Bible's categories are concrete and personal: the widow, the fatherless, the stranger, the hired servant defrauded of his wages, the poor man whose cloak is kept overnight. The principle to recover is that God hears actual cries from actual sufferers and requires actual justice — ye shall not respect persons in judgment, neither the person of the poor nor the person of the mighty.

Greek & Hebrew Roots

Hebrew ts'āqâh is an outcry wrung out by distress; sh''âh is a cry for help; rinnâh is a ringing cry, whether of joy or entreaty. Greek krazō is to cry out with a loud, raw voice, and boaō is to call aloud.

expand to see more

Hebrew ts'āqâh (H6818) — an outcry, shriek of distress; the cry of Israel under the taskmasters (Exo 3:7) and the cry of Sodom.

Hebrew sh''âh (H7775) — a cry for help, entreaty; let my cry come unto thee (Psa 102:1).

Hebrew rinnâh (H7440) — a ringing or resounding cry; used of both jubilation and supplication, as attend unto my cry (Psa 17:1).

Greek krazō (G2896) — to croak, shriek, or cry out; whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15), and the cry of the blind man Christ stopped for.

Greek boaō (G994) — to call or shout aloud; the voice of one crying in the wilderness (Mat 3:3).

Usage

"Of the cry God hears and acts upon: I have heard their cry by reason of their taskmasters; for I know their sorrows (Exo 3:7)."

"Of the rule of God's dealings: the righteous cry, and the LORD heareth, and delivereth them (Psa 34:17)."

"Of the Spirit's cry in the believer: the Spirit of adoption, whereby we cry, Abba, Father (Rom 8:15)."
